title: Bridge – rules
sub: The queen of card games: four players in two partnerships, 52 cards and 13 tricks. First you bid how many tricks you can win – then one partner lays their hand face up on the table.
goal: The goal: bid a contract with your partner and win at least as many tricks as you promised – or stop the other pair from making theirs.

seo.rulesT: Bridge rules – how to play Contract and Rubber Bridge

info.gearAlt: A deck of 52 playing cards, paper and pen
info.intro: Bridge has been played around the world for a century – from kitchen tables to Olympic mind-sport halls. Every deal has two halves: a short auction where pairs bid for the right to name trumps, and 13 tricks where one partner becomes the Dummy and lays all their cards face up.

rules.setupLead: Bridge is played by exactly four players in two fixed partnerships: North–South against East–West. Partners sit directly across from each other.
rules.tableAlt: Bridge table layout: North and South sit opposite each other as one pair, East and West sit opposite each other as the other pair, with 13 cards each.
rules.rankLead: Use a standard 52-card deck with no jokers. Inside every suit the cards run straight from 2 (lowest) up to Ace (highest).
rules.rankAlt: Card order from lowest to highest: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, jack, queen, king, ace.
rules.dealP: The dealer shuffles, lets the player to their right cut, and deals the entire deck clockwise, one card at a time, starting to their left. Everyone holds 13 cards. After each deal, the role of dealer moves one seat clockwise.
rules.bidLead: Before the first card is played, both pairs bid to decide two things: which suit is trump (or No Trump) and how many tricks the winning pair must take. The five strains rank from lowest to highest:
rules.lvlP: Every bid pairs a level (1 to 7) with a suit or NT. The first 6 tricks are called the book and don't count on their own; your bid states how many tricks above 6 your pair promises to win. So 1♠ means 7 tricks (6 + 1), 4♥ means 10 tricks, 6NT means 12 tricks (Small Slam) and 7♠ means all 13 tricks (Grand Slam).
rules.b1p: The dealer speaks first, then turns go clockwise. On your turn you may make a higher bid, say Pass, Double an opponent's last bid (raising the stakes) or Redouble if an opponent doubled your pair's bid.
rules.b2p: A new bid must be at a higher level (like 2♣ over 1♠) or in a higher strain at the same level (like 1♥ over 1♦, or 1NT over 1♠). Passing does not lock you out – if someone bids later, you may bid again on your next turn.
rules.b3p: If all four players pass right at the start, the hand is thrown in and the next dealer deals again. Once any bid has been made, three consecutive passes end the auction. The final bid becomes the contract.
rules.b4p: In the winning pair, whoever first named the contract's trump suit (or NT) during the auction becomes the Declarer – even if their partner made the final bid. Declarer's partner becomes the Dummy; the other two players are the Defenders.
rules.aucAlt: Example auction: North opens 1 heart, East passes, South raises to 2 hearts, West passes, North bids 4 hearts, followed by three passes.
rules.aucNote: North–South reach a contract of 4♥ (10 tricks with hearts as trump). Because North named hearts first, North is Declarer, South is Dummy and East leads the first card.
rules.playLead: With the contract set, the table plays 13 tricks clockwise. One rule makes Bridge unlike almost any other card game: one whole hand lies face up for everyone to see.
rules.t1p: The defender sitting to Declarer's left plays the first card face up onto the table.
rules.t2p: Immediately after the opening lead, Dummy places all 13 cards face up in four neat columns by suit (trumps on Dummy's right). From now on Dummy stays silent: Declarer plays both hands, choosing their own cards and calling which card Dummy plays each trick.
rules.t3p: Everyone plays one card per trick in clockwise order. You must follow the suit led if you hold any card of it. If you can't follow suit, you may play a trump (ruff) or discard any other card – there is no obligation to trump or to beat the highest card.
rules.t4h: Win the trick and count to 13
rules.t4p: The highest trump wins the trick; if no trump was played (or in No Trump), the highest card of the suit led wins. The winner takes the trick and leads next – if Dummy won, Declarer leads from Dummy's cards. After 13 tricks, count how many tricks Declarer's pair won.
rules.trickAlt: Example trick in a 4 hearts contract: East leads king of spades, South plays 4 of spades from Dummy, West plays ace of spades, North ruffs with 3 of hearts and wins.
rules.trick2: Dummy follows with the 4 of spades (called by North)
rules.trick3: follows with the ace of spades
rules.trick4: has no spades and ruffs with the 3 of hearts
rules.trickNote: Even the tiny 3 of hearts beats the ace of spades because hearts are trump. North wins the trick for North–South and leads to the next one.
rules.scLead: At home tables Bridge is classically scored as Rubber Bridge. Draw a line across a notepad: points for contracted tricks go below the line (toward Game); bonuses and penalties go above the line.
rules.sc1: Minor suits (♣ / ♦) – below the line, per contracted trick
rules.sc2: Major suits (♥ / ♠) – below the line, per contracted trick
rules.sc3: No Trump (NT) – below the line (1st trick 40, each extra 30)
rules.sc4: Game – 100+ below the line in one or more deals (3NT, 4♥/♠, 5♣/♦)
rules.sc5: Small / Grand Slam – above the line, bid & made (non-vul)
rules.sc6: Rubber bonus – above the line, first to 2 games (2–0 / 2–1)
rules.sc7: Undertricks – to defenders above the line, per trick (non-vul / vul)
rules.scP: Only the tricks you bid and make count below the line. Extra tricks (overtricks) go above the line at the same rate (20 for ♣/♦, 30 for ♥/♠/NT when undoubled) – so you only win a Game in one deal if you actually bid it. Once a pair reaches 100 below the line, draw a new line under both columns and start the next Game at zero. When a pair wins two Games, add up everything above and below the line: the highest total wins the rubber.
rules.vulP: A pair that has already won one Game in the rubber is vulnerable. Their slam bonuses jump to 750 (Small Slam) and 1500 (Grand Slam), while their undoubled undertrick penalties double from 50 to 100 per trick. If a contract is doubled, trick points below the line count double (plus a 50-point bonus above for making it, 100 redoubled), while overtricks and penalties climb steeply.
rules.scExP: North–South bid 4♥ (non-vulnerable) and take 11 tricks. They score 4 × 30 = 120 below the line (winning a Game right away!) plus 30 above the line for the one overtrick. If they had only managed 9 tricks (down 1), North–South score nothing and East–West enter 50 points above the line.
rules.varLead: Bridge is played in clubs, living rooms and hostels around the world. If you want a shorter session or an easier first night, try one of these formats:
rules.var1: Chicago (Four-Deal Bridge): Play exactly four deals instead of a full rubber – about 20 minutes. Deal 1 nobody is vulnerable; Deals 2 and 3 only the dealer's side; Deal 4 both pairs. Part-scores don't carry over between deals; making a Game scores +300 (non-vul) or +500 (vul).
rules.var2: Duplicate Bridge: The tournament and club format. Multiple tables play the exact same pre-dealt hands from card boards and compare scores, removing card luck almost completely.
rules.var3: Mini-Bridge: Perfect for total beginners. Skip the bidding: everyone announces their High Card Points (A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1), the stronger pair sees both hands, and the partner with more points simply picks trump (or NT) and Part-score or Game.
rules.var4: Honors bonus (Rubber): Holding 4 of the 5 top trump honors (A, K, Q, J, 10) in one hand scores 100 above the line; all 5 in one hand (or all 4 aces in NT) scores 150.
rules.var5: Five or six players (cut-in): Everyone draws a card; the lowest one or two sit out the first rubber. After each completed rubber, waiting players rotate in so the whole group plays together.
rules.faq1q: What does “the book” mean in Bridge?
rules.faq1a: The first 6 tricks won by Declarer's pair. Bids only count tricks above 6, so a bid of 1♣ commits you to 7 tricks (6 + 1), and 3NT commits you to 9 tricks (6 + 3) – see Bidding.
rules.faq2q: Does the person who made the last bid always play the hand?
rules.faq2a: No. Declarer is whichever player in the winning partnership first named the contract's trump suit (or No Trump) during the auction. If South bids 1♠ and North jumps to 4♠, South is still Declarer and North is the Dummy.
rules.faq3q: Can I bid again if I already passed?
rules.faq3a: Yes. Passing only skips your current turn. If another player makes a bid, the auction continues and you are free to bid, pass or double when your turn comes back around.
rules.faq4q: Do I have to trump if I can't follow suit?
rules.faq4a: No. Unlike some European trick-taking games, Bridge has no obligation to trump or to beat the highest card on the table. You only have to follow the suit that was led if you can.
rules.faq5q: Can the Dummy give advice or help play the cards?
rules.faq5a: No. Once Dummy lays their 13 cards face up, Declarer controls both hands alone. Dummy simply moves the exact card Declarer names – and may only warn Declarer if they are about to lead from the wrong hand or accidentally fail to follow suit.
rules.faq6q: What happens if we win more tricks than we bid?
rules.faq6a: You make your contract and score the extra tricks as overtricks above the line. However, overtricks never count toward the 100 points needed for Game – so bidding 3♥ and taking 10 tricks scores 90 below and 30 above, not a Game.
rules.faq7q: How do I know what to bid as a beginner?
rules.faq7a: Start by counting High Card Points (A=4, K=3, Q=2, J=1): open with 12+ points, look for an 8-card fit in hearts or spades, and aim for Game from 25 combined points. See the strategy guide and the quick start cheat sheet.
rules.faq8q: How long does a game take, and can we play a quick round?
rules.faq8a: A full Rubber usually takes 30 to 60 minutes depending on how fast Games are won. For a fixed 20-minute round, play Chicago (four deals) – see Variants.

strategy.sub: Bridge rewards planning far more than lucky cards. Count your points, talk clearly with your partner in the auction, and pause for ten seconds before you play trick one.
strategy.principle: Bridge is two linked skills: bidding finds the right contract, and card play squeezes every possible trick out of it. Great players don't memorize a hundred conventions – they master a handful of reliable habits.
principleItems: Bidding is a partnership language. You aren't bidding your own hand in isolation – you are describing your strength and shape so the two of you can find a fit and the right level.
Never touch a card at trick 1 before making a plan. The opening lead is on the table, Dummy is face up – you now see 26 of the 52 cards. Pause and plan the whole deal first.
Defense wins just as many points as declaring. Half the deals you'll defend. Good leads and simple partner signals turn impossible contracts into easy defeats.
strategy.evalLead: Before you bid, count your High Card Points (HCP). The top four cards in each suit are worth:
strategy.evalP: Every suit holds 10 HCP, so the entire deck has 40 HCP and an average hand holds 10. Combine your estimate with what your partner's bids promise:

ladder.label: Opening hand – strong enough to open the bidding at the 1-level

strategy.fitP: Don't forget length (the 8-card fit): If you and your partner hold at least 8 cards together in hearts or spades, you have a trump fit. Long suits (5+ cards) and short side suits (a singleton or void) create extra ruffing tricks, making your hand worth more than its raw HCP.
strategy.bidLead: You don't need complex systems to bid well at any table. Five simple guidelines cover most deals:
bidItems: Open 1 of a suit with 12–21 HCP. With a 5-card major (♥ or ♠), open 1♥ or 1♠. Without one, open your longest minor (1♣ or 1♦ – with two 3-card minors, open 1♣).

Open 1NT with 15–17 HCP balanced. A balanced hand has no void, no singleton and at most one doubleton (shapes 4-3-3-3, 4-4-3-2 or 5-3-3-2 without a 5-card major). One bid tells partner both your exact strength and your shape.

Respond to partner's opening with 6+ HCP. Never leave partner stranded at the 1-level if you hold 6 or more points: support partner's major with 3+ cards, show a 4+ card suit of your own at the 1-level, or bid 1NT with 6–9 HCP and no fit.
Prefer 4♥, 4♠ and 3NT over 5♣/5♦. Taking 9 tricks in 3NT or 10 in a major is far easier than scrambling for 11 tricks in clubs or diamonds.
Stop once you know the ceiling. If partner opens (12–14) and you hold 8 points (20–22 combined), settle for a safe part-score instead of pushing to Game.
strategy.exAlt: Example 13-card hand: spades A K 10 8 4 (7 HCP), hearts Q 6 3 (2 HCP), diamonds K J 2 (4 HCP), clubs 7 5 (0 HCP). Total 13 HCP with five spades, so open 1 spade.
strategy.exWhy: Why 1♠? You have 13 HCP (above the 12-point opening mark) and a strong 5-card major. Even though the hand is semi-balanced (5-3-3-2), it's below the 15–17 range for 1NT – so 1♠ immediately tells partner you have opening strength and at least five spades.
strategy.decLead: The moment Dummy hits the table, resist the urge to play a quick card. Follow a four-step checklist:
decItems: Count Winners in No Trump. Add up your immediate top tricks (aces, kings with the ace, solid sequences). Subtract from your contract – that tells you how many extra tricks you must build, usually by attacking your longest combined suit.

Count Losers in a Suit Contract. Look at your hand (the longer trump hand) and count likely losing cards in each suit. Then ask how to eliminate them: trump losers in Dummy, discard them on Dummy's long winners, or take a finesse.

Draw trumps early – unless you need ruffs. In most suit contracts, pull opponents' trumps first so they can't ruff your aces and kings. Delay drawing trumps only when you first need Dummy's trumps to ruff your losers.
High card from the short hand first. Holding A–K in one hand and Q–J–10–4 in the other? Cash the A and K from the shorter side first so you don't block the suit and strand the rest.
Watch your entries. Keep a high card in Dummy as a bridge to reach its winners later – don't accidentally cash Dummy's only entry before the long suit is set up.
strategy.finAlt: Finesse diagram: Dummy leads 4 of spades toward Declarer's ace and queen of spades. East plays 7 of spades, and Declarer plays the queen of spades to trap the king if East holds it.
strategy.finWhy: How the finesse works: You hold A♠ Q♠ and are missing the K♠. Instead of banging down the Ace (which wins only 1 trick), lead a low spade from Dummy toward your A–Q. If East plays low, put in the Q♠: whenever East holds the K♠ (50 % of the time), your Queen wins and your Ace wins next – two tricks instead of one!
strategy.defLead: Defenders can't see each other's hands, so clarity beats cleverness. Five classic rules take you a long way:
defItems: Against No Trump: lead 4th-highest from your longest suit. Holding K–J–8–5–2? Lead the 5. You protect your honors while racing to establish your small cards as winners.

Against a Suit: lead sequences, singletons or partner's suit. Leading the top of touching honors (K from K–Q–J) is the safest lead in Bridge. Avoid leading away from an Ace in a suit contract – Declarer's King might score for free.

Second hand low, third hand high. When Declarer leads a low card, play low in second seat so you don't waste an honor. In third seat (when partner led), play your highest card to force out Declarer's stopper – or the lowest of touching honors (Q from K–Q).
Return partner's suit. When you gain the lead, usually send back the suit your partner led at trick 1 – they chose it for a reason.
Read the Dummy. Dummy sits open in front of you: lead through Dummy's strong suits (when Dummy is on your left) and up to Dummy's weak suits (when Dummy is on your right).
mistakes: Playing instantly from Dummy at trick 1. Rushing the first card without counting winners or losers is the #1 cause of going down in makeable contracts.
Forgetting to draw trumps. Leaving opponents with stray trumps lets them ruff your best side-suit aces and kings.
Aiming for 5♣ or 5♦ when 3NT is on. Winning 9 tricks in No Trump is much easier than taking 11 in a minor – check for stoppers and play 3NT whenever you can.
Passing partner's 1-level suit opening with 6–9 HCP. Partner might hold 19 points! Always keep the auction alive with 6 or more points.
Leading an unprotected Ace (or underleading an Ace) against a suit contract. Cashing a lone Ace often sets up Declarer's King and Queen.
Cashing the long hand's honors first. Always unblock the shorter hand first, or you'll trap winners in Dummy with no way to reach them.

quick.rule: 4 players (N–S vs E–W), 13 cards each. 1) Bid level 1–7 (= 6 + tricks) and trump/NT; 3 passes set the contract. 2) Play: left of Declarer leads, Dummy lays hand face up, Declarer plays both. 3) Score tricks below, bonuses above the line.
quick.suitsNote: Lowest → highest in bidding · right column: cheapest 1-deal Game (100+ pts).
quick.rankNote: Must follow suit if able. Can't follow? Ruff with trump or discard freely – no obligation to trump or beat.
